title: Nowhere to put the feet
hookLine: a potter taps each saint's head, and an old man won't keep his feet off the linga
carry: nowhere to put the feet where God is not

cards: A potter walks down a row of seated saints, holding the flat wooden paddle he uses on pots. He taps a pot and listens: fired all the way through, or still soft inside?
The story says Jnaneshwar asked him, Gora the potter, to test the devotees gathered there. So Gora taps each head. Each saint sits quietly and takes it.
Then he reaches Namdev, and Namdev bristles, and says so. Gora listens, and tells the whole room: this pot is still half-baked.

teach.b: That stung, because Namdev's love for Vitthal was real.
So he runs to Vitthal to complain. And Vitthal, in the story, takes the potter's side. You have love, he says.
What you don't have yet is a teacher. Go and find Visoba Khechar.
Namdev finds the old man asleep in a Shiva temple, his feet resting on the linga, the stone that stands for Shiva. Shocked, Namdev wakes him. I'm old and tired.
Lift my feet, please, and set them down somewhere God is not. Namdev moves them. A linga rises up under them.
He moves them again. Another. Wherever the feet come down, Shiva is already there.
At last Namdev sets them in his own lap, and he understands: there is nowhere to put the feet, because there is nowhere without God.

It's one of Hinduism's oldest teachings: the Isha Upanishad opens by saying that all this, whatever moves in the world, is pervaded by the Lord. So what was wrong with the pot? Not too little devotion.

Devotion with walls around it, so fond of God in one image, in one town, that it couldn't see him anywhere else. Hindus take care not to point their feet at a shrine, out of respect. Visoba isn't mocking that respect.
He's showing where it leads: if God is everywhere, every place deserves it. All week, a mango, a song, a buffalo, a wall, a bowl of milk: wherever the saints looked, God was already there.

how: The stories of Gora the potter and Visoba Khechar belong to the Varkari tradition of Maharashtra, whose members sing the songs of Namdev and the other saints of Pandharpur in praise of Vitthal.

games.q: you're Namdev. an old man lies with his feet on the Shiva linga, and asks you to set them down somewhere God is not. what do you do?
o: refuse and walk out of the temple.
lift his feet and set them down somewhere else.
go and fetch the temple priest.
games.why: he moves them again and again, and a linga rises under them each time, until he understands there's nowhere without God.

practice: Bring to mind one ordinary place you'll be later: a bus seat, a sink full of dishes, a waiting room. Set your attention down there gently, the way Namdev set down those tired feet, and ask: what if God is already here too?
If you pray, you can hold that place before God. If you don't, simply plan to treat that place, for one moment, with the care you'd give a shrine.

wordCard.voice: Namdev. The poet-saint of Pandharpur, called half-baked by a potter, who learned from Visoba Khechar that there's nowhere to put the feet where God is not.

carryVoice: Your line: nowhere to put the feet where God is not. Tomorrow: a dog runs off with Namdev's bread. why does he chase it with butter? A week, done.
